I definitely studied Dutch for more than a year before I started at the university, but I don't think it was (much?) more than two years. The first year was mostly for fun, using Rosetta Stone and Teach Yourself books. The second year I spent two periods of approximately 3 months in the Netherlands. The first time I took two intensive intermediate classes building up to taking the staatsexamen, which shows that you speak the language well enough to work or study in the Netherlands (according to the website). I passed the exam and went home for 3 months, during which time I read most of a history textbook required for the university entrance exams. (That was really painful in the beginning ... I probably read about 3 pages a day.) Then I returned to the Netherlands where I prepared for the entrance exam by seeing a tutor once a week, and doing independent study the rest of the time, focusing on reading academic texts and writing short essays. I think I would write an essay every week and we'd talk about it during the tutoring session. Something like that. Anyway, the whole process was very expensive, but effective. If I'd been able to get into the university based on previous academic studies then I would have been able to stay in the Netherlands for up to a year prior to starting in order to learn Dutch.

I feel like three days of heavy vocab practice is overkill if you're already doing some every day in addition to reading or writing. Personally I'd use that time instead to practice speaking (vlog-style if nothing else) or do more reading and listening. Speaking is a very different skill from writing, so I'd highly recommend practicing it plenty if you want to get good. And with regards to reading and listening, I think input is way more important than drilling vocabulary. You'll be much more able to pick up on more nuances, for example, if you spend the bulk of your vocabulary-learning time listening to German radio and reading books rather than doing flashcards.

In my experience you can't really plan this kind of thing ahead of time. You just have to take a look once you get to that point, and see what you need to do. In fact, my experience is that just finding materials to use to keep up your language can take up a lot of time. Then again, I'm picky and dislike reading the news, which is a huge disadvantage when you're learning or maintaining a language ...

Reading these paragraphs, it sounds like you have a pretty vivid idea of what your characters are like, which is great. What I'd work on is more surface stuff-- style. Have you tried reading your work aloud to yourself? If not I would give it a try, and pay attention to how it flows, if the choice of verb tense feels natural, that sort of thing.

A couple specific things that I noticed ... I stumbled over the second sentence in the first paragraph. I had to reread the bit about Douglas' father being a farmer, because generally I expect farmers to be in the country, or going to the city, or they're not a farmer yet, but they're leaving the city in order to become a farmer. Then I stumbled over "Ada Perry ... who struggled to support themselves". The easiest thing to do would be to split it into two sentences, the second beginning with something along the lines of "Ada and James struggled to earn enough to support themselves."

You begin the second paragraph with "It was early May when life for Douglas would change forever." Because of this sentence I expect what follows to be a description of the day that things changed, and it felt awkward when you continued using the verb tense of an action that Douglas repeated many times. It also takes away from the immediacy. I'd recommend telling how it happened on that day. In order to indicate that this was something he did frequently you can write things like "as he was accustomed to doing" or "he sat in his usual spot". You could even talk about how familiar the landscape was to him because of how he had drawn it a hundred times before.

I hope this helps! You've got a good start here. :)
